location: Abdulhai et al. (2026) [c174] table row (report line 69); report-data.json status_by_cid.c174
claim: c174 is recommended for the core dataset (status_by_cid.c174 = "core").
problem: The supported status is context: the reported diversity comparisons use observational subgroups defined by actual AI use, and the separate revision study compares AI-generated with human-generated output. In S1, access to AI was randomized, but the qualifying diversity result compares heavy-use and light-use subgroups separately with controls, not the full randomized AI-access arm with the control arm. Specifying the subgroup rule before analysis does not randomize actual use. The creativity rating is self-reported and cannot supply the missing qualifying outcome. No other study supplies a qualifying randomized-arm comparison.
evidence: Independently read Abdulhai et al (2026) - How LLMs Distort Our Written Language.pdf: PDF p. 4, section 3.1, randomizes no-LLM versus AI access; p. 5 classifies actual users as LLM-Influenced or LLM using self-reported text generation checked against transcripts. PDF pp. 8-9, Figure 4b and section 4.2, compare the heavy-use cluster and light-use distribution separately with controls; Figure 4a and section 4.1 identify creativity as self-report. PDF pp. 5-6 describe researchers generating revisions of archived human drafts for the AI-versus-human comparison. forms/c174.json studies[0].outcomes[0].measure_detail explicitly states "Actual-use subgroups split the randomized AI-access arm; no combined AI-access-versus-control estimate is printed"; its contrasts name those two subgroups, while studies[0].outcomes[4].scored_on_output is false. Nevertheless eligibility.core and final.core are "yes". The codebook sections 1 and 3 require an output-based creativity/diversity outcome for randomized human assistance and designate AI-versus-human output as context.
